weaknesses: Needed strong interviewer guidance to recall max heap / priority_queue.
Needed guidance to discover the sorted-capital + forward-pointer optimization.
Clarifying questions were mostly skipped at the start.

rewrites.original: Each step, I choose 1 projects with biggest profits among selections affordable with w capital that are unselected before.
rewrites.better_spoken_english: At each step, I choose the unselected project with the highest profit among the projects I can currently afford.

rewrites.original: In each k step, I need to scan all n items to find project in specific condition.
rewrites.better_spoken_english: In each of the k iterations, I would have to scan all n projects to find the most profitable project that is currently affordable.

rewrites.original: we don't need to scan them, since they can't be selected. the w is not enough to start the projects.
rewrites.better_spoken_english: We don’t need to scan the remaining projects because the list is sorted by capital, so none of them can be afforded with the current capital.

rewrites.original: I used sort and max heap for selecting max profit in each step among the items whose capitals are lower than current capital.
rewrites.better_spoken_english: I sort the projects by required capital and use a max heap to select the highest-profit project among all projects I can currently afford.

revealed_pattern: Greedy + sorting by eligibility threshold + max heap (priority queue) + monotonic forward pointer
selection_reason: Randomly selected as part of the weekly Hard x2 set. In hindsight, it is useful interview practice for maintaining a changing set of eligible candidates and repeatedly selecting the best one.
recognition_signals: Repeatedly choose the maximum/minimum among currently eligible candidates.
Eligibility is controlled by a threshold such as required_capital <= current_capital.
The threshold only moves forward, so sort once and sweep with a pointer.
Previously eligible but unchosen candidates must remain available for later rounds.
Brute force repeatedly rescans all candidates at every step.

questions: How do I store (capital, profit) pairs?
Can I use vector<vector<int>> instead of pair?
How can I sort the project list?
implementation_questions.notes: sort(projects.begin(), projects.end()) compares the first inner value first, so capital is the primary key.

questions: What is a normal max heap in C++?
What happens if top() or pop() is called on an empty heap?
implementation_questions.notes: priority_queue<int> is a max heap by default. Use push/top/pop/empty.

questions: If i is initialized from pointer, does i keep changing when pointer changes?
Why does a forward-only pointer prevent rescanning?
implementation_questions.notes: i and pointer are separate variables; pointer only moves forward.

questions: Why add sequential complexities instead of multiplying them?
Does O(k*n + n log n + k log n) simplify to O(n^2) when k <= n?
Are constants also dropped in space complexity?
implementation_questions.notes: Final optimized complexity is O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

transcript.text: Problem understanding: inputs are k, w, profits, capital; choose up to k projects to maximize final capital, subject to minimum capital requirements.
Clarified that profit is added to current capital rather than replacing it.
Proposed greedy selection: at each step choose the highest-profit currently affordable unselected project.
Asked what repeated work causes O(k*n), then guided toward maintaining already-affordable projects.
Considered categorizing projects by capital and using maps; could not yet identify the best structure for repeatedly selecting maximum profit.
Gradually prompted toward a max heap / priority_queue.
Guided toward sorting projects by required capital and scanning them with a forward-only pointer as w increases.
Worked through examples and understood that all newly affordable profits are pushed to the heap, while unchosen profits remain there.
Asked about heap insertion/deletion complexity, sorting complexity, Big-O constant removal, and sequential vs nested complexity.

Asked implementation questions about vector<vector<int>>, pair alternatives, initializer lists {}, sort, lexicographical order, #include syntax, snake_case, priority_queue, push_back, and pointer behavior.
Submitted initial C++ implementation using a sorted project list, priority_queue<int>, pointer, and k iterations.
Pointed out that without stopping at the first unaffordable sorted project, later projects are unnecessarily rescanned.
Added `if (pairs[i][0] > w) break;` and understood why this avoids worst-case repeated O(k*n) scanning.
Dry-ran k=2, w=0, profits=[1,2,3], capital=[0,1,1] and corrected the final capital to 4.
Handled the edge case where no project is initially affordable and the heap remains empty.
Concluded final optimized complexity is O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
Submitted the final C++ implementation with early break and empty-heap check.
